cards.title: Architecture: the RIMS archival pipeline's eight stages
questions: how is the rims archival pipeline architected
walk me through the eight stages of the archival pipeline
rims pipeline architecture
what are the stages of the rims pipeline
how do the archival pipeline stages hand off to each other
eight stage pipeline design
format lanes in the archival pipeline
how does she structure a multi stage archival processing system
how did you design the stages and gates for the archive pipeline
what does each rims stage own
architecture of the university library archival system
how are different file types routed in the archival pipeline
what happens to emails versus images versus documents in the archive build
cards.answer: Eight stages joined by one manifest, each with a named owner, a gate condition that defines done, and a stated dependency on the stage before it: 00 source and access, 01 inventory and identify, 02 triage and appraisal, 03 extraction and routing, 04 enrichment, 05 metadata, 06 index, search and delivery, 07 scale and scheduling. The manifest is one row per file path, stored as partitioned Parquet, and each stage adds the columns it owns, which is what makes a mixed accession processable at all. Inside extraction, files go down format lanes, email, image, document, tabular and scientific, rather than one path. My standing rule there: where a fact is already in a file header, a model only phrases it, never discovers it. The September 2026 demonstration processed 2,375 real files across three accessions in about 21 seconds on 4 vCPU, with the review interface on top.

cards.title: Turning three proofs of concept into one production system
questions: how do you take several proofs of concept into one production system
how did you unify three proofs of concept
poc to production architecture
what had to change to move the archival work from prototype to production
consolidating prototypes into one pipeline
why port com automation to tika and libreoffice
what blocked the archival prototypes from production
how do you turn a demo into an operational system
proof of concept to production transition
how do you consolidate several pilots into one platform
cards.answer: Find the shared representation first, then remove the dependencies that can't scale. The archival production build merged three proofs of concept, image classification, email processing and file search, which had three corpora and no shared vocabulary. The unifying piece is a single manifest every stage reads and writes. Then I treated blockers as design inputs. The file-search prototype drove Word, Excel and PowerPoint through COM automation, which can't run on Colab or the Linux GPU server, can't be parallelized safely and hangs on malformed files, so porting to Tika plus headless LibreOffice is a prerequisite, with output parity checked against the prototype on the same files. The image work's throughput limit came off first: moving to vLLM took a full 12,125-image pass from about 22 hours to about 3.7. Each inherited prototype folder also got a README saying what's reusable and what's known to be broken.

cards.title: Multi-tenancy and per-user data isolation
questions: how do you handle multi tenant concerns

tenant isolation

cards.answer: Honestly, I haven't built a multi-organization SaaS. The legislative platform serves one institution with per-user isolation inside it. Cosmos DB holds each user's profile, tracked bills, categories, impact prompts and scores under a partition-key schema shared by the live app and the nightly scorer. The move that makes it scale per user is decoupling: bill features are extracted once per bill, and impact scoring runs per user against their own prompts, so adding a user never re-extracts the corpus. Sharing is explicit, team-wide versus named individual, and every AI briefing is bound to the user whose lens produced it. The closest thing to multi-tenant design is Legacy, a personal project, where every record carries a userId and every storage path is user-scoped, so opening it to other users is an additive change.

cards.title: Multi-agent system architecture: one queue, lanes and rails
questions: walk me through your multi agent system architecture
how is your agent system architected
29 agents shared queue memory decision log
why one job queue for all agents

how does the queue decide when work starts

what rails do the agents share
how do you orchestrate many agents on one workstation
the scheduling layer of your agent system
cards.answer: I run 29 agents across Skyrule and my other personal projects on one workstation with one GPU (as of October 2026), organized like a small company: each has a written charter saying what it owns and what it doesn't. They share four rails: one job queue, one memory, one decision log and an ownership map that tooling enforces. The queue is the only thing that launches work, so "why did this run now?" always has one logged answer; the cost is that the queue becomes critical infrastructure, so I kept it small, file-based and tested. Lanes are statements about shared resources, each with its own concurrency limit: 4 for CPU scripts, 1 for vLLM because speed comes from batched requests inside a run, and a budgeted Claude lane. Jobs carry dependencies, start conditions and finish checks that decide done by evidence rather than exit code.

cards.title: Sharing one GPU across models and workloads
questions: how do you share one gpu across multiple models
gpu scheduler design
gpu lease
what happens when vllm and ollama compete for the gpu
how do you stop two models fighting over vram
one model on the gpu at a time
gpu contention between workloads
how did you get two pipelines to share one server
co-locating workloads on a single gpu
how do you switch models on a single card safely
model swapping on limited vram
cards.answer: I make the GPU a lease with exactly one holder. In my personal agent system, a vLLM server reserves 94% of the RTX 5090 and a 32B Ollama seat needs about 20 GB, so they can't share, and when they collide Ollama doesn't fail loudly; it spills to the CPU and runs about ten times slower. So the card is idle, one vLLM profile, or the Ollama seats, never two. A switch never interrupts running GPU work: it's refused and asked again on the next tick. After every switch the result is checked against actual memory use and server health, never assumed. Time windows for who holds the card, generation overnight and agents by day, still run as a dry run. Evidence Desk follows the same rule at work: one model resident on the GPU at a time.

cards.title: Architecture of a self-improving system: Drop Radar
questions: how does drop radar improve itself
self improving system architecture
how does the feedback loop rewrite its own code
self modifying agent design

self healing system design
how did you design the drop radar agent loop

cards.answer: Drop Radar, a personal project, improves itself from its user's texts, and the architecture is a loop with gates. Anything sent to the Telegram bot that isn't a command is saved to a feedback inbox. A file watcher notices a new note, or a source that has started failing, and queues a run of a dedicated Claude Code agent with written rules and a living knowledge file. The agent diagnoses the issue, edits the code or source configuration, runs the tests, restarts the service and replies with what changed. The gates: 25 tests on fabricated data, a live on and off flag for every extra feature so anything declined comes out without a restart, and a weekly check-in with Keep, Change and Drop buttons per change. One bug taught me the watcher must compare note identities, not counts: a new note went unnoticed because the open count hadn't changed.

cards.title: Model lifecycle: two clocks, auto-pickup and one input path
questions: how do you architect retraining and rescoring
prediction freshness versus model freshness
how often do you retrain versus rescore
two independent clocks daily rescore monthly retrain
how does a new model get into production
model deployment without code changes
train serve shared input module
model lifecycle management
how do you promote a retrained model
retraining cadence design
how do you keep a production model current
cards.answer: I separate prediction freshness from model freshness and run them as two independent clocks. For bill passage prediction, a daily run rescores active bills through the current model as new actions land, and a monthly retrain refreshes the model on full history with recency weights. The daily job picks up a new model file automatically, no code change, and the introduction-time model was built the same way: it activates on the server when its model file is present. Conflating the two clocks means either stale predictions or needless retraining. Inputs go through one shared module used by both training and nightly scoring, after I found the two formatting inputs differently; 36,028 inputs now verify byte-identical. And versions get pinned: re-pulling a moved "latest" tag silently changes the model you evaluated.

cards.title: Architecting an enterprise copilot over internal documents
questions: how would you architect an enterprise copilot over internal documents
enterprise rag copilot design

how would you build an ai assistant for executives

citation backed chatbot
cards.answer: I'd start from three decisions: what it may see, who it answers for, and how a reader checks it. On the legislative platform, retrieval is hybrid, MiniLM embeddings in FAISS alongside structured filters, and the Legislative Assistant, built on Microsoft's Copilot agent framework with GPT-4.1, returns citation-backed, structured answers. I set the retrieval standards up front, embedding selection, metadata indexing and incremental updates, along with citation and interpretability requirements for executive trust. Who it answers for is a profile: each user's title, functional area, stakeholders and interests are injected into the prompt, so the same bill reads as a budget issue for one person and an AI-ethics question for another. For sensitive collections, my archival version 2 design keeps everything local: a 30B-class model on vLLM, BGE-M3 embeddings, FAISS or Qdrant, no external calls.

cards.title: Designing a team layer around an AI attribution risk
questions: how did you design the team collaboration layer
sharing ai briefings between users
human versus ai attribution
how do you stop an ai misrepresenting a colleague
foia risk in ai systems
how do you label ai generated content in a shared workspace
team sharing and annotations design
governance risk in collaborative ai tools
how do users correct what the ai says about them
collaboration features in the legislative platform
how do readers know which content is ai generated
cards.answer: I designed it around a governance risk identified in advance: an AI characterizing a named colleague's position slightly wrong, inside a FOIA-able system, at a public university. So the architecture holds a hard line between human and AI attribution. Every machine-generated briefing is badged as AI-authored and bound to the user whose lens produced it, so a model's interpretation is never mistaken for a colleague's stated position. Shares are team-wide or to a named individual, the distinction is stored and shown, and individual shares and flags sort above broadcasts. Imports can be untracked reversibly, so a mistake costs no data. The mitigation adopted is that users own and can correct any extracted characterization of their own view before others see it, and those corrections double as training signal for the planned institutional-memory capability.

cards.title: Schema decisions that are free now and costly later
questions: which architecture decisions are expensive to retrofit
what decisions did you make early because they are hard to change later

what is the gating architectural choice for the digest agent

one way door decisions

cards.answer: I sort roadmap work by adoption cost, and I look hard for the schema decisions that are free now and prohibitively expensive later. On the legislative platform the clearest one is attribution: extraction must bind every claim to a person, a timestamp and the verbatim source sentence from day one, because reconstructing who held which position after the fact would mean reprocessing the entire corpus. Second, position records as the durable artifact. Discussion is raw material; what gets retrieved years later is the institutional position, the reasoning, who was in the room and what changed their mind. Third, for the planned digest agent, I framed the deployment choice, precomputed nightly on on-prem vLLM versus generated live on managed cloud inference, as the gating architectural decision rather than an implementation detail.

cards.title: Designing an email intake channel
questions: how would you design an email intake channel
email intake dossiers

committee hearing alerts design

cards.answer: Ask for the smallest behavior change possible and let existing infrastructure do the routing. For the legislative platform I designed per-bill dossiers fed by an intake mailbox that users simply CC. The institution's most valuable legislative analysis already lives in email threads and is lost when those threads are archived. Inbound mail would be matched to the right bill through the platform's existing semantic matching, and email carries sender identity for free, so every contribution arrives attributed. Pointing the same mailbox at the clerk's committee postings turns a manual phone-call process into a push feed for hearing alerts: one mechanism for two of the three most-cited stakeholder pain points. To be clear, it's designed and on the roadmap, scoped in follow-up meetings, not built yet.

cards.title: Where an agent belongs in a pipeline, and at what granularity
questions: where do agents belong in a pipeline
when should you use an agent versus a classifier
agent loop per file or per folder
local domain expert agent for archival appraisal
how would you design an agentic layer on top of a pipeline
agent cost at corpus scale
rims version 2 agent
agentic appraisal design
how do you scope an ai agent in a batch system
agents versus workflows in architecture
how do you keep agents affordable at corpus scale

cards.answer: Where judgment is needed, and at the coarsest level that still works. For the archival pipeline's version 2, I scoped a fully local agent that scans an ingested drive, builds an understanding of the owner's subject domain, and ranks files for archival value, sensitivity and review priority with written explanations an archivist can evaluate. The constraint I wrote into version 1: agent loops belong at folder and collection level, not per file, because an agent loop costs many model calls where a classification costs one, and at corpus scale that's hours versus weeks. Anything a deterministic step or a single classification can do stays outside the agent; if the task doesn't require interpreting something undefined, it isn't agent work. The proposed stack stays on the network: a 30B-class model on vLLM, a vision-language model, BGE-M3, FAISS or Qdrant, controlled filesystem access.

cards.title: Architecture review: what I'd change in my own systems
questions: what would you change in your own architecture in hindsight
what would you do differently architecturally
architecture review of your own systems
design mistakes you would fix
if you started the agent queue again what would change
what are the weaknesses of your architecture
known limits of your systems
what did you get wrong in the design
regrets in system design
what technical debt would you pay down first
critique of your own designs
what is the weakest part of your systems
which design choices would you redo
cards.answer: A few, all from things that bit me. My agent job queue keeps over a thousand jobs in one JSON file guarded by a lock file and rewrites the whole list on every change; I'd use SQLite from day one. It detects usage limits by matching text in job output, which once paused a lane for a day when an agent's own report mentioned the limit; the real fix is a structured exit signal. Shell writes are guarded by heuristics, so I'd run each agent in a sandbox where out-of-scope paths simply aren't writable. On the legislative pipeline I'd make success falsifiable from the start: a stage could report green with zero output, and one malformed bill looped as a poison pill for six days. And the probability trail's monotonicity fix belongs in the model, not the display layer.

cards.title: Where approval gates sit in an autonomous system
questions: where do you put human approval gates in an autonomous system
approval gates for ai automation
authority levels for agents
dry run flag and test recipient redirect
how do you roll out autonomous emails safely
receipt gated release chain

how do you stop agents publishing without approval

cards.answer: I gate by consequence: the more public or irreversible the action, the closer the gate sits to a person. The legislative digest shipped behind a dry-run flag and a test-recipient redirect, and go-live waited for in-person onboarding. In my personal agent system I wrote down three authority levels: agents fix isolated bugs alone, a department head approves bounded changes, and only I decide spending, release scope, sensitive data and public deployment. No agent publishes; the shell guard denies every git push. Release steps are receipt-gated, so each starts only when its predecessor's receipt carries the exact result the gate reads. At work, the archival program-manager agent holds proposed GitHub updates for human review.

cards.title: A reference architecture for a first production LLM system
questions: what reference architecture would you propose for a company's first production llm system
reference architecture for llm
how would you design a mid size company's first ai system
blueprint for a production llm application
what would your default ai stack be
starter architecture for generative ai
how would you set up llm infrastructure from scratch
first llm system in production design
what does a good first ai platform look like
your go to architecture
default architecture for an llm product
components of a first llm deployment
cards.answer: Assembled from what has worked for me. Start with a small open model on one owned GPU behind vLLM with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and a config-driven router so the backend can change without code changes. Put deterministic code in front: exact matches, hash-based change detection, cheap filters, so the model only sees what survives. Store artifacts as Parquet with one schema contract per stage, and make every write idempotent and resumable. Route by sensitivity, volume and latency: sensitive and bulk work local, small interactive calls to a managed API, with results cached per input. Let code copy evidence and compute numbers; the model picks and judges. Give every job a standard log schema and a monitor that checks output counts, not exit codes. Ship behind dry-run flags and test recipients, and measure on your own documents before anyone calls it accurate.

cards.title: Observability for a multi-agent system
questions: how do you observe a multi agent system
how do you know what your agents are doing
agent city architecture
how does agent city get its state
monitoring dozens of agents
the overseer agent
agent status dashboard design
how do you show which agents are stuck
deterministic state projection
why poll instead of push for the agent dashboard
observability for autonomous agents
which agents need my attention
cards.answer: With 29 agents and hundreds of jobs, logs stopped answering "who is working, who is stuck, who is waiting on me?", so I built Agent City, a personal project: a 3D town in the browser that is a read-mostly projection of the real system. It owns no scheduling and runs no work. Each agent carries a few authoritative fields, and one pure function maps them to a single displayed state with fixed precedence: blocked, waiting on me, working, queued, offline, paused, scheduled soon, sleeping, idle. An unreachable runtime shows as offline, never asleep, and tests check every conflicting pair, so "working" means a job is actually running. Browsers poll every 5 seconds with a cursor, which is simple and holds up on a standard-library server. Separately, an hourly Overseer round checks every agent for failed, stuck or vanished runs, and never acts.

cards.title: Designing a safe control surface for autonomous jobs
questions: how do you design controls for an autonomous system
run now button that cannot bypass gates
idempotency keys for commands
how do you stop a dashboard from becoming a way around the rules
safe ui controls for agents
command preview and confirm design
double tap on phone creates duplicate job
append only done log
control plane design for agents
how do commands from the town reach the queue
preventing duplicate jobs from double clicks
cards.answer: Every control in a UI has to pass the same gates as everything else. In Agent City, my personal agent dashboard, "run now" sets aside one date gate on one queued job and records the original; it's refused for approval flags, dependencies and start conditions, and it never overrides a usage pause or the launch budget. Every command can be previewed without changing anything. Commands that spend usage, override a gate, pause or cancel need an explicit confirm. The same idempotency key within 24 hours returns the stored result and never creates a second job, so a double tap on a phone is harmless. Running jobs are never touched. The town's few writes go through the queue's own lock, and because queue records can be pruned or rewritten, the town appends each finished job once to an append-only Done log. Access is private-network only.

cards.title: Receipt-gated release chains for long generation runs
questions: receipt gated job chain
how do you gate a long llm generation run
canary runs for llm generation
gpu kill switch supervisor
how do you stop a failed step being run past
release engineering for generated content
quarantined canary protocol
how do you supervise unattended gpu runs
wall clock backstop
how are verification passes bound to code versions
safeguards for overnight gpu runs
how do you stop a pipeline skipping a failed check
releasing a large batch of generated content
cards.answer: For long, expensive generation runs I chain steps on receipts, not on exit codes. In Skyrule, my personal project, every chain step starts only when its predecessor's receipt JSON carries the exact result the gate reads, so a failed step can't be run past. Releases go through a quarantined canary on a frozen, dated protocol with acceptance gates set in advance. Canary 1 failed its 50-piece two-grader check at 18 of 50, and the five generator habits behind it became validator checks. A supervisor with a wall-clock backstop stops generation at a cutoff, verifies the model server is down and restores the standing server, while a connection watch attributes every client touching the model port by Windows job-object membership. Each verification is bound to the code hashes it tested, so an old pass can't open a gate after a change.

cards.title: Designing outputs that carry their own reasons
questions: how do you design outputs people can argue with
why expose the probability trail instead of a single score
explainability by design
storing the reason next to the result
momentum badge design
per person explainability output
why does each file show its ranking reason
how do you make predictions inspectable
transparent outputs architecture
audit friendly outputs
showing users why something ranked where it did

explaining to users why an item ranked high
cards.answer: I design outputs so a person can argue with them, which usually means storing the reason next to the result. The legislative passage model writes a per-action probability trail, 432,262 rows, as a first-class artifact rather than one score per bill. The trail drives the in-app curve and the momentum badge, which compares the last three actions with the prior three, and it exposed a monotonicity defect that a single current value would have hidden. In the archival triage ledger, every file shows why it ranked where it did, quoted from the archivist's own intake form, and folder-level inclusion stays a separate stated reason rather than being blended into one number. The retirement forecast emits per-person explainability: raw score, age prior, comparable cases, the shrunk estimate, the floor, and which mechanism moved it.

cards.title: Designing for unattended operation
questions: how do you design systems that run unattended

how do you keep a scheduled service from dying silently

cards.answer: I design for the hours nobody's watching, which mostly means honest launches and honest health. In my personal projects, jobs launch only from the scheduled task, never from a chat session, after a session-launched job died with its console. Drop Radar's loop stopped twice in one day because the scheduled task opened a visible console that a stray Ctrl+C could kill, so it moved to a hidden launcher with an auto-restart wrapper. Health has to mean it worked: the Discord feed counts as healthy only if a post actually arrived in the last 24 hours, and a watcher raises a Telegram alarm when no source has been checked for 30 minutes; it fired 34 minutes into a real outage. A periodic hook may queue work only from an allowlist of scripts and arguments, at most hourly, so editing config can't run an arbitrary command.

cards.title: Building human review into the pipeline: the Accession Workbench
questions: how do you architect human review into an ai pipeline
accession workbench
triage ledger design
append only decision log for reviewers
how do archivists review machine decisions

review interface for ai triage
bulk review actions with sensitive items excluded

cards.answer: Review is part of the architecture, so it gets a real surface and a real record. The archival pipeline's Accession Workbench puts a triage ledger in front of the archivist: every file shows its generated title, a two-sentence summary, folder location, flags and its ranking reason. Decisions can be made per file or a whole band at a time, with sensitive material automatically excluded from bulk actions. Decisions go into an append-only log, where changing your mind writes a second entry pointing at the first, because "selected at 14:02, changed at 14:19" is the record an archive needs. Three release versions, original, reading room and open web, sit side by side, so the archivist chooses what publishes rather than trusting a setting. A review pass returned 481 decisions, each stamped with its reviewer, and exposed a real rationale-field bug.

cards.title: Scaling the archival pipeline: compute, layout and agent cost
questions: what breaks first when the archive pipeline scales
scaling the archival pipeline to millions of files
how long would 100000 images take
five million row manifest
why are embeddings stored outside the manifest
dataframe fragmentation at scale
archive scale capacity
what changes at five million files
how does the rims design scale
sizing the archival workload

cards.answer: Scale shows up in three places: compute, data layout and agent cost. Compute: under Ollama a full 12,125-image pass took about 22 hours; on vLLM with the same L4 it takes about 3.7, and a 100,000-image collection moves from 12 to 13 days to about 30 hours with no new hardware. Data layout: at five million rows, 384-dimension embeddings are about 7.5 GB, so they live outside the manifest as pointers, and building roughly a hundred columns one at a time fragments the DataFrame, harmless at five rows and severe at five million. Agent cost: loops belong at folder and collection level, because per-file loops turn hours into weeks. And the biggest lever, the free-filter reduction, has to be measured on a complete drive before any of this sizing is trusted.

cards.title: Hosting and IP protection for a consumer AI product
questions: how did you choose hosting for skyrule
skyrule production architecture

digitalocean postgresql vercel clerk stripe

cards.answer: For Skyrule, my personal project, the hosting plan follows one rule: valuable machinery stays server-side. The decided plan is a stateless FastAPI container on a DigitalOcean droplet with managed PostgreSQL, the web front end on Vercel, Clerk and Stripe, and an iOS app that's a thin client. The IP-protection plan backs that up with per-account rate limits, traceable delivery logs and trade-secret practice, informed by research I ran on client decompilation, API scraping and model distillation. The internal API is locked down on a reviewed branch: authentication on every route, no prompt or rule-file exposure, closed CORS, rate limits. Privacy shapes the data layer too: users' personal chart data never goes to a cloud model, consent gates storing anyone else's data, and the database plan includes deletion and export. It's pre-beta, so this is decided architecture, not yet load-tested.

cards.title: Content addressing and hashing as an architecture tool
questions: how do you use hashing in your architectures
content addressing
deterministic file ids blake2b
content hash change detection
fingerprinting requests and scorers
how do you know two runs used the same inputs
stable identifiers across re crawls
hash based incremental processing
why hash everything
sha 256 receipts
proving two runs were the same test
cards.answer: I use hashes wherever "is this the same thing?" has to be answered by code. In the archival manifest, file_uid is a blake2b hash over source identifier plus normalized path, so a re-crawl yields identical keys and manifest generations join; exact duplicates collapse by content hash in the free-filter tier but stay recorded as duplicate_of rather than deleted. The legislative pipeline's change feed is a content hash per artifact, so a quiet day does almost no work, and nightly impact scoring re-evaluates only bills whose hash changed. Evidence Desk fingerprints frozen case manifests, requests, client settings and scorers with SHA-256, and the merge tool refuses anything that doesn't match. In my personal agent system, every memory stores its source file's hash, and gate passes are bound to the code hashes they tested.

cards.title: Architecture of a personalized AI digest
questions: how is the personalized email digest built
digest architecture
how do you design a personalized ai briefing email
weekly digest function design
what goes into each user's digest

digest cadence daily weekly real time
personalized newsletter generated by ai
digest agent design

how is each stakeholder's email assembled
cards.answer: A digest is a scheduled assembly job over a user's own lens, so the lens is data and the schedule is a function. On the legislative platform a timer-triggered Azure Function assembles each recipient's digest from their profile, impact prompts, saved categories and tracked bills, and delivers it through managed email on their chosen cadence: daily, weekly or real-time. I designed the structure as state over time: headline finding, baseline framing, tracked bills, other movers, most imminent items, the macro picture, and a count of watched items with no material change. The first edition establishes a baseline and later editions report only what changed. The next design step is a digest agent that curates by reasoning across all of a user's signals instead of filtering on thresholds, where the deciding question is nightly on-prem precompute versus live cloud generation.

cards.title: Skyrule's system architecture: code computes, the model writes
questions: walk me through skyrule's architecture
skyrule system design
how is skyrule layered

versioned fastapi engine and rule store
provenance first architecture
how do you keep an llm from inventing facts in a product
designing a product where the model cannot invent facts
cards.answer: Skyrule, my personal project, is layered so that anything factual is computed by code and the model only writes. At the bottom is a deterministic Python engine exposed through a versioned FastAPI layer, with regression controls that must reproduce 279 reference spans exactly. Above it is a rule store built by a provenance pipeline over a 76-title licensed corpus: extraction, independent verification by a second model, a verbatim-quote gate and page re-checks, so every rule traces to a book, a page and a quote. The relationship model is explicit functions with 206 weights held in a ledger, deliberately producing no total or compatibility score. Generation is brief-then-prose: code lays out what's supported, a local model plans claim by claim, code validates every claim, then the model writes one sentence per approved claim and code checks again.

cards.title: Architecting a shared server for many production pipelines
questions: how do you architect a shared server for many pipelines
linux analytics execution environment

keeping pipelines from interfering with each other on one server
what infrastructure do your pipelines run on
cards.answer: I treat one shared server as a platform with conventions, because several production pipelines run on it at once: legislative processing, proposal NLP, archival image classification, the retirement forecast and more. Each gets its own environment. vLLM 0.6.6 lives in an isolated conda environment because the system Python carries a different vLLM and an incompatible syntax surface, so serving runs in the vLLM environment and the benchmark scripts in system Python; the retirement forecast runs in its own virtual environment. Every pipeline writes the same Parquet logging contract, so one monitor sees all of them. Shared resources get managed explicitly: right-sizing the language model's GPU allocation freed about 15 GB so the archival pipeline could share the L4, and after an out-of-memory failure took down the shared JupyterHub, I moved heavy jobs off it.

cards.answer: On October 26 I folded Skyrule's 14 agent departments into five working teams: Foundation, Platform, App & Brand, Release and Program. The goal was fewer deciders, with records staying in their department homes. The departments survive as review hats, and each team's write scope is generated as the union of the hats it wears, never wider; the agent-definition folder and the live site stay out of every team's scope. I tested the change like code: 31 build checks including a planted out-of-scope control, guard self-tests at 45 of 45 and 27 of 27, and 12 live allow and deny checks. Alongside it came an append-only status log with a single locking writer, self-tested with four writers appending 25 lines at once and none interleaved, a daily morning-brief PDF built from files with no model, and a 30-minute stall watch.

questions: how do you control model spend in an agent system

agent cost governance
rate limiting your own ai agents
how do you keep agents from running up a bill
rationing an expensive model across agents
what happens when you run out of model usage
cards.answer: I treat model usage as a shared resource with its own lane and its own ledger. In my personal agent system the Claude lane spends my own usage, so it's opt-in per job: a job without an approval note never starts there. A weekly budget, enforced by the queue from its own launch log, caps launches so at least half my weekly usage stays free for my own work, and every raise is recorded with my reason. Unattended Claude jobs are capped at two at a time, while the GPU and CPU lanes are unmetered. When Claude reports a usage limit, the whole lane pauses until the stated reset, and that stop doesn't count as a failed attempt. The gap I'd close: cost is tracked as launches against the budget, not as tokens.

cards.title: Designing per-user lenses: profiles, impact prompts and categories
questions: how did you design personalization in the legislative platform
per user impact scoring design
user profile injected into the prompt
custom impact prompts
why not one institution wide impact score
personal lens architecture
how do users customize what the ai looks for
custom keyword categories
token limits on user written context
personalized ai analysis design
analysis tailored to each person's job
cards.answer: I started from a premise: a single institution-wide impact score is too broad to act on, because impact only means something relative to a person's role. So on the legislative platform each user defines a lens and the system applies it to every active bill. The profile, title, functional area, stakeholders served and the legislation they watch for, is injected into the LLM prompt for every downstream analysis. Users write impact questions in their own words, and each is scored against every active bill on a No, Low, Moderate or High scale with a one-sentence rationale. Up to ten keyword categories each choose which fields they search. I built explicit token and input-length limits into the profile and prompt interfaces so user-written context can't silently truncate the model's input, and explained the reason to users.

cards.answer: I put it where the team already talks and kept every write behind review. For the archival build I set up a shared program-manager agent in Microsoft Teams to track progress and blockers and link chat updates to GitHub issues, with proposed GitHub updates held for human review before anything changes. I drafted its acceptance criteria: shared access, reading a designated chat, accurate issue matching, duplicate prevention and reviewed GitHub updates. Then I report against them honestly. It opens in Teams, and GitHub issue retrieval and designated-chat retrieval have been demonstrated; automatic monitoring, persistent duplicate prevention and GitHub writes remain unverified. It sits on a repository built as the single source of truth, with 33 open issues across stages 00 to 07 and Blocked as a board column rather than a label.
